Subject: Re: Discovery — performance targets and next steps

Jamie — thanks again for the call earlier. Quick recap and a few clarification items so we can align the SLO language and produce a short SLA draft for procurement/legal. High level goals you shared:

- P95 response latency goal for user-facing flows ~150ms (server-side)
- Peak concurrency ~200 concurrent live chat sessions; average burst to 400 for 5–10 minute windows
- Streaming responses for chat (token-by-token) required for best UX
- Throughput estimate: ~1.2M tokens/day across peak US region

Action items from Redwood side: produce an SLO definition document that specifies exactly how latency is measured (service edge vs client), exclusions (maintenance, force majeure, customer-side network), reporting cadence, and remedies for breaches. Attached is a first-pass SLO draft I mentioned (MediLink_SLO_Draft.pdf).

Questions for you to confirm:
1) Do you want P95 or P99 as the primary contractual metric?
2) For streaming, do you require continuous streaming (chunked transfer) for 100% of chat traffic, or is best-effort acceptable with fallbacks to non-streaming?
3) Any blackout windows or maintenance windows that should be excluded from availability calculations?

Next steps: If you confirm the two metrics above, Marcus from our infra team will follow up with precise measurement language and a proposal for reporting cadence. I’ll loop in Legal/Procurement on the SLA draft once we confirm.

Thanks — Rishi

Rishi — thanks for the summary and the draft. A few clarifications from our side:

- We’d prefer P99 as the contractual latency metric for critical API calls (session init + first 3 response tokens) because our clinical UI is sensitive to tail latencies. P95 is acceptable as an operational metric but procurement will push for P99 in the SLA.
- Streaming: we need token-by-token streaming for the chat feature for 95% of interactions during normal operation. For high-load fallbacks, non-streaming is acceptable but should be explicitly called out as a degraded experience.
- Blackouts: we have weekly maintenance windows (Sat 02:00–04:00 PST) where traffic is expected to be low and prefer those excluded. Any customer-induced rate-limiting (our side) should be excluded.

Attaching a quick network diagram showing our frontend proxies and expected egress points (mediLink_network_diag.png).

If you can send measurement language for P99 and streaming behavior, we’ll share with Procurement/Legal and get back with redlines.

—Jamie

From: Marcus Lin <marcus@redwoodinference.com>

Subject: RE: Discovery — performance targets and next steps

Jamie — good notes. Below is the measurement language Redwood proposes for inclusion in the SLO/SLA draft. This is intended to be explicit (we prefer to avoid ambiguity in contracts):

1) Latency definition (per-request):
- Measurement point: latency is measured at Redwood’s service edge (the point where a request is accepted by the Redwood ingress load balancer and a 200/4xx/5xx response is emitted by the Redwood service).
- Metric: time from receipt of initial client request to first byte of application response (TTFB) for streaming-enabled requests we also capture time-to-first-token and time-to-last-token.
- Aggregation: P99 measured over a rolling 30-day window for contract purposes; P95 reported weekly for operational visibility.

2) Concurrency/Throughput:
- Concurrency: measured as number of active sessions with an open model execution (i.e., KV cache + session state) at a given time, sampled at 1s intervals.
- Throughput: measured in tokens/sec and tokens/day at the Redwood edge.

3) Streaming behavior:
- Streaming success: a streamed response is considered successful if the server emits token chunks continuously with no >500ms gap between tokens for the first 75% of tokens in the response.
- Fallbacks: when falling back to non-streaming due to load, Redwood will mark the request as "degraded"; degraded requests count against availability but are reported separately in monthly reports.

4) Exclusions and windows:
- Excluded from SLA calculations: planned maintenance windows (mutually agreed, e.g., Sat 02:00–04:00 PST), force majeure events, customer-side network outages (e.g., failed DNS resolution on customer proxies), and any third-party provider outages documented by provider status pages.
- Emergency maintenance: Redwood will notify 30 minutes prior when possible; emergency maintenance may be excluded if it meets the agreed criteria below.

5) Measurement tooling and clock sync:
- Redwood uses server-side timestamps synchronized via NTP; customer-side tracing instrumentation may be used for joint investigations but not for contract adjudication unless both parties agree to a shared measurement approach.

6) Reporting cadence and remedies: 
- Reporting: Redwood will produce a monthly SLO report with P99/P95 numbers, token throughput, concurrency samples, streaming success rate, and a list of incidents affecting the month. On request, a CSV export of request-level samples will be provided for the prior 30 days.
- Remedies: standard service credit table applies for P99 breaches (credits computed as % of monthly invoice tiered by severity). Payment/credit mechanics will be set in the SLA annex.

Attached: redwood_slo_measurement_note.txt — short version of the above for the SLA annex.

Please confirm the P99 target, acceptance of the maintenance window exclusion, and whether you want the streaming success criteria tightened (e.g., 300ms gaps vs 500ms). Once we align, I’ll draft the SLA language for Legal to review.

—Marcus
